instructions: Thinly slice the 2 onions. Melt 1 tbsp of the butter with 1 tbsp of the oil in a large heavy pot over medium. Add the onions and cook them for about 20 minutes, stirring every few minutes, and turn the heat down to medium low once they've wilted. They're ready when they're soft, deep golden and smell sweet. Don't rush the onions. That's where the flavor starts.

Meanwhile, cut the 1.5 lb beef into 1 1/2 inch cubes and pat them dry with paper towels. Sprinkle them with the 1/2 tsp salt and the 1/4 tsp pepper, then toss them with the 1 tbsp flour until every side has a light coat.

Heat the remaining 1 tbsp butter and 1 tbsp oil in a large skillet over medium high. Add half the beef in one layer and leave it alone for 3 to 4 minutes, until the underside is deep brown and lets go of the pan. Turn the cubes and brown the other sides the same way, then move them to a plate. Brown the second half of the beef the same way.
Pour 1/2 cup of the broth into the hot skillet and scrape up all the browned bits with a wooden spoon. Turn off the heat.

Mince the 2 garlic cloves and grate the ginger. Add them to the onion pot with the 1 tsp curry powder and the 1 tbsp tomato paste. Stir for about 1 minute, until it smells fragrant and the paste turns a shade darker.

Add the beef with its juices and the liquid from the skillet. Peel the carrot, cut it into big chunks and add it, then pour in the remaining 2 1/2 cups broth. Bring it to a boil over medium high and skim off any gray foam with a spoon.

Grate a quarter of the apple straight into the pot and stir in the 1 tbsp Worcestershire and the bay leaf. Cover, turn the heat to low and simmer for 1 1/2 hours, stirring now and then. If the liquid drops below the beef, add a splash of water.

About 40 minutes before the beef is done, start the rice. Rinse the 2 cups rice in a strainer under cold water until the water runs mostly clear. Put it in a saucepan with 2 1/4 cups water and bring it to a boil over high heat. Turn the heat to low, cover the pan and cook for 15 minutes. Take it off the heat and keep the lid on until you're ready to serve.

Peel the 2 potatoes and cut them into 1 1/2 inch chunks. When a fork slides into the beef easily, add the potatoes, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, until a knife goes into a potato with no push. Fish out the bay leaf and turn off the heat.
Break off half the box of roux. Put 2 cubes in a ladle, dip it into the pot and stir with a spoon until they melt, then stir that into the curry. Repeat until that half of the roux is in.

Turn the heat to low and simmer for about 5 minutes, until the sauce is thick enough to coat a spoon. Keep stirring along the bottom the whole time, or it'll catch and burn. If it gets too thick, stir in a splash of water.
Taste it. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Spoon the rice onto one side of each plate and the curry onto the other. Leftover curry keeps for 3 days in the fridge. Store it apart from the rice and reheat it on low with a splash of water.
method_notes: Just One Cookbook (beef) and Adam Liaw both brown floured or seasoned chuck in batches, simmer it until tender with carrot, potato and a grated apple, and season with ketchup or tomato paste and Worcestershire. Just One Cookbook caramelizes the onions first, deglazes the beef pan with red wine and finishes with a store-bought roux off the heat; Adam Liaw makes his own butter and flour roux with curry powder and simmers 1 to 1 1/2 hours. Just One Cookbook's chicken version skips the long braise and cooks thighs for about 20 minutes. This one follows the beef version at a 1 1/2 hour simmer, deglazes with broth instead of wine, and uses half a box of mild roux for four.
